summary: Scott Wu opens by reflecting on the rapid pace of AI software engineering, suggesting conferences should occur every two months. He introduces 'Moore's law for AI agents,' measuring capability by how long an AI works uninterrupted before requiring human intervention. General AI doubling time is approximately seven months, but code-specific tasks double every ~70 days, yielding 16-64x annual capacity growth. Eighteen months ago, only tab completion had product-market fit in coding; now full AI engineer agents exist. Wu emphasizes that the most important capability, optimal interface, and primary bottleneck all shift every 2-3 months as agents reach new tiers. He traces Devin's evolution through multiple tiers. First (summer last year): repetitive migrations like JS-to-TS conversions, requiring reliable step-by-step execution across thousands of files. Cognition built 'playbooks' for instruction following and a knowledge/memory system. Second (early fall): isolated, intern-level bugs and features requiring repository snapshots and clean remote VMs running CI and linters. Third (fall): broader cross-file changes requiring codebase understanding via call hierarchies, language servers, and git commit history. Slack integration became central, and Devin went GA. Fourth (spring this year): as tasks grew harder, humans no longer knew everything upfront, so two-line prompts were insufficient. Cognition released Deep Wiki, exposing Devin's internal codebase representation to humans, and 'with search' for asking codebase questions. An iterative L2 workflow emerged: explore the codebase with the agent, then assign the task. Devin 2.0 introduced an in-IDE experience where users closely monitor Devin for 10-20% of a task and let it work autonomously for 80-90%. Fifth (June): the ability to handle entire backlogs autonomously, requiring confidence to distinguish understood tasks from ones needing human help, plus async self-testing where the agent runs code locally, knows what to test, and iterates. Looking ahead, Wu sees the next frontier as tackling entire projects. He stresses that while all 2x improvements look similar in retrospect, each requires fundamentally new capabilities—from single-line text prediction to human collaboration, planning, autonomous testing, and debugging. He predicts another 16-64x improvement over the next 12 months.

sections.title: Opening and Moore's Law for AI Agents
sections.summary: Scott Wu introduces Moore's law for AI agents: capability measured by uninterrupted work before human intervention. General AI doubles every ~7 months, but code tasks double every ~70 days, yielding 16-64x annual improvement. 18 months ago only tab completion had PMF in coding; now full AI engineer agents exist. The key bottleneck and interface shift every 2-3 months at each new tier.

sections.title: Tier 1: Repetitive Migrations and Playbooks
sections.summary: Around summer last year, the first broadly adopted use case was repetitive migrations (JS to TS, Angular/Java version upgrades) across thousands of files with clear step sequences. Cognition built 'playbooks' for reliable instruction following and a knowledge/memory system to accumulate human feedback across repeated tasks.

sections.title: Tier 2: Isolated Intern-Level Bug Fixes
sections.summary: By early fall, agents could handle isolated, intern-level bugs and features. Cognition built repository snapshots and clean remote VMs that could run CI and linters, enabling basic validation. Devin positioned as a 'junior buddy' delivering broader value beyond migrations.

sections.title: Tier 3: Broad Cross-File Changes and GA Launch
sections.summary: In fall, Devin tackled broader bugs requiring cross-file changes of hundreds of lines. Key capability: understanding code as hierarchy via call hierarchies, language servers, and git commit history. Slack integration became central for assigning issues. Devin went GA during this period.

sections.title: Tier 4: Deep Wiki, Codebase Search, and Devin 2.0
sections.summary: By spring, harder tasks meant humans no longer knew everything upfront, making short prompts insufficient. Cognition released Deep Wiki, exposing Devin's internal codebase representation to humans, and 'with search' for asking codebase questions. An iterative L2 workflow emerged: explore the codebase with the agent first, then assign the task. Devin 2.0 introduced an in-IDE experience where users monitor Devin for 10-20% of a task and let it work autonomously for 80-90%.

sections.title: Tier 5: Autonomous Backlog Handling and Future Outlook
sections.summary: In June, Devin gained the ability to handle entire backlogs autonomously, requiring confidence to distinguish understood tasks from ones needing human help, plus async self-testing where the agent runs code locally and iterates. Wu notes each 2x doubling is fundamentally different in practice, evolving from text prediction to human collaboration, planning, testing, and debugging. The next frontier is entire projects, with another 16-64x improvement predicted over 12 months.
